questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Behavior of a Function in the Neighborhood of a Point
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13980965/assets/5143df65d0f99c6511dc8ab13262831669c88535e19c986dacdb364e04847f58.png)

Which of the following statements are true with respect to the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is plotted above. 

- $f(x)$ is defined at $x=2$
- ${lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)\ne f(2)$
- $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=2$
questions.worked_solution:
By inspecting the graph, we can conclude the following:

- Statement I is true. We have $f(2)=2.$

- Statement II is false. Indeed, from the graph we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{-}}f(x) & =2, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}f(x) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)=2=f(2).$

- Statement III is false. The graph of the function doesn't have a break at $x=2$ and we can draw the graph of $f(x)$ around $x=2$ without taking our pencil off of the paper.

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following statements are true? 

- $f(x)$ is defined at $x=5$
- ${lim}_{x\to \,5}f(x)$ exists
- $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=5$
questions.worked_solution:
By inspecting the graph, we can conclude the following:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, $f(5)=2.$

- Statement II is false. Indeed, from the graph we see that

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{5}^{-}}f(x) & =2, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{5}^{+}}f(x) & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,  ${lim}_{x\to \,5}f(x)$ doesn't exist

- Statement III is true. The graph of the function has a jump exactly at $x=5$
and it's impossible to draw the graph without taking our pencil off of the paper.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13980965/assets/8086893e4587e68f8257b75f2070cf622fa141199d6bd8960f7c4fd8e7bcb349.png)

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following statements are true? 

- $f(x)$ is **not** defined at $x=0$
- ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)$ exists
- $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=0$
questions.worked_solution:
By inspecting the graph, we can conclude the following:

- Statement I is true. From the graph we can see that no value has been assigned to $f(x)$ at $x=0.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}f(x) & =3, \\ {lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}f(x) & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 
${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=3.$

- Statement III is false. The function is not even defined at $x=0.$ The graph contains a break at $x=0.$ It's impossible to draw the graph of $f(x)$ without taking our pencil off of the paper.
